title: Moroccan Lamb Tagine with Apricots
shortDescription: Tender lamb slow-cooked with warm spices, dried apricots, and almonds
note: Serve with fluffy couscous to soak up the fragrant sauce
introCopy: This classic Moroccan tagine balances savory lamb with sweet apricots and warm spices like cinnamon and ginger. The slow braising creates fall-apart tender meat in a silky sauce.

steps.text: Heat olive oil in a tagine or heavy-based pot over medium-high heat. Brown lamb pieces in batches until golden on all sides. Remove and set aside.
Reduce heat to medium. Add onions and cook until softened, about 8 minutes. Add garlic and cook for 1 minute.
Stir in cumin, coriander, ginger, cinnamon, and saffron. Cook until fragrant, about 1 minute.
Return lamb to the pot. Add tomatoes and stock. Bring to a boil, then reduce heat to low. Cover and simmer for 1.5 hours.
Add apricots and honey. Continue simmering uncovered for 30 minutes until lamb is very tender and sauce has thickened.
Season with salt and pepper. Garnish with toasted almonds and fresh coriander. Serve over fluffy couscous.

title: Classic Moroccan Chicken Tagine with Preserved Lemons
shortDescription: Aromatic chicken braised with olives and tangy preserved lemons
note: The preserved lemons are essential for authentic flavor
introCopy: This iconic Moroccan dish features chicken slow-cooked with briny olives and the unique tang of preserved lemons. It's one of Morocco's most beloved tagines.

steps.text: Heat olive oil in a tagine or large pot over medium heat. Brown chicken pieces on all sides, about 8 minutes. Remove and set aside.
Add onion to the pot and cook until softened, about 5 minutes. Add garlic, ginger, turmeric, and saffron. Cook for 1 minute.
Return chicken to pot. Add stock and bring to a boil. Reduce heat, cover, and simmer for 45 minutes.
Add preserved lemons and olives. Continue cooking uncovered for 15 minutes until chicken is very tender and sauce has reduced.
Season with salt and pepper. Garnish with fresh coriander and serve with couscous.

title: Moroccan Vegetable Couscous
shortDescription: Seven-vegetable couscous with chickpeas and aromatic broth
note: Traditionally served on Fridays in Morocco
introCopy: This vegetarian couscous royale features seven vegetables symbolizing good fortune, simmered in a fragrant broth and served over fluffy couscous with chickpeas.

steps.text: Heat olive oil in a large pot or couscousier. Add onions and cook for 5 minutes until softened.
Add cumin, coriander, turmeric, and cinnamon. Cook for 1 minute until fragrant.
Add carrots, turnips, squash, stock, and tomatoes. Bring to a boil, then reduce heat and simmer for 20 minutes.
Add chickpeas, courgettes, and cabbage. Continue simmering for 25 minutes until all vegetables are tender.
Season with salt and pepper. Stir in fresh coriander.
Fluff couscous and mound on a large platter. Arrange vegetables on top. Ladle some broth over the couscous. Scatter with raisins if using. Serve remaining broth alongside.

title: Harira - Moroccan Lentil Soup
shortDescription: Hearty tomato-based soup with lentils, chickpeas, and fresh herbs
note: Traditionally breaks the fast during Ramadan
introCopy: This fragrant Moroccan soup is rich with lentils, chickpeas, tomatoes, and warming spices. Often served with dates and chebakia during Ramadan.

steps.text: Heat olive oil in a large pot. Add onion and celery, cook until softened, about 8 minutes.
Add lamb and brown on all sides, about 5 minutes. Add ginger, turmeric, cinnamon, and pepper. Stir for 1 minute.
Add lentils, chickpeas, tomatoes, and stock. Bring to a boil, then reduce heat and simmer for 40 minutes until lentils and lamb are tender.
Mix flour with 100ml cold water to make a smooth paste. Stir into soup to thicken. Add vermicelli and cook for 5 minutes.
Stir in fresh coriander, parsley, and lemon juice. Season with salt. Simmer for 5 more minutes.
Serve hot with additional lemon wedges.

title: Tunisian Shakshuka
shortDescription: Eggs poached in spicy tomato and pepper sauce
note: Best served with crusty bread for dipping
introCopy: Tunisia's version of shakshuka features harissa for heat and is packed with peppers and tomatoes. Perfect for breakfast, lunch, or dinner.

steps.text: Heat olive oil in a large deep frying pan over medium heat. Add onion and peppers, cook for 8 minutes until softened.
Add garlic, harissa, cumin, and caraway seeds. Cook for 1 minute until fragrant.
Add tomatoes and simmer for 10 minutes until sauce has thickened. Season with salt and pepper.
Make 6 wells in the sauce. Crack an egg into each well. Cover and cook for 5-6 minutes until whites are set but yolks still runny.
Scatter with feta if using and fresh parsley. Serve immediately with crusty bread.

title: Moroccan Pastilla with Chicken
shortDescription: Sweet and savory pie with spiced chicken, almonds, and phyllo
note: A showstopper dish for special occasions
introCopy: This elaborate Moroccan pie balances sweet and savory with layers of spiced chicken, toasted almonds, eggs, and cinnamon sugar, all wrapped in crispy phyllo pastry.

steps.text: Heat olive oil in a large pot. Cook onions until softened, 8 minutes. Add chicken, garlic, ginger, cinnamon, saffron, and stock. Simmer covered for 35 minutes until chicken is very tender.
Remove chicken and shred finely. Return to pot with coriander. Reduce liquid over high heat until nearly evaporated, about 10 minutes.
Add beaten eggs to the chicken mixture. Stir constantly over low heat until eggs are scrambled and mixture is dry, about 5 minutes. Set aside to cool.
Mix ground almonds with icing sugar and cinnamon. Set aside.
Preheat oven to 180°C. Brush a 30cm round baking tin with butter. Layer 8 sheets of phyllo in the tin, brushing each with butter and letting edges overhang.
Spread half the chicken mixture over phyllo. Top with almond mixture, then remaining chicken. Fold overhanging phyllo over the filling.
Top with 6 more buttered phyllo sheets, tucking edges down into the tin. Brush top generously with butter.
Bake for 35-40 minutes until golden and crisp. Let rest 10 minutes, then invert onto a serving platter.
Dust with icing sugar and make decorative cinnamon lines across the top. Serve warm, cut into wedges.

title: Merguez Sausages with Peppers
shortDescription: Spicy lamb sausages with roasted peppers and harissa yogurt
note: Serve in flatbreads for an authentic street food experience
introCopy: These fiery North African lamb sausages are loaded with cumin, paprika, and harissa. Paired with sweet roasted peppers and cooling yogurt, they're utterly addictive.

steps.text: Preheat oven to 200°C. Toss peppers and onions with olive oil and cumin on a large baking tray. Season with salt and pepper.
Nestle merguez sausages among the vegetables. Roast for 25 minutes, turning sausages halfway, until sausages are cooked through and vegetables are charred.
Meanwhile, mix yogurt with harissa and lemon juice. Season with salt.
Serve merguez and peppers in warm flatbreads with harissa yogurt and fresh coriander.

title: Chermoula Baked Fish
shortDescription: White fish marinated in herb and spice paste, then baked
note: Chermoula also works brilliantly with prawns or chicken
introCopy: Chermoula is Morocco's zesty marinade packed with coriander, parsley, lemon, and spices. It transforms simple white fish into something spectacular.

ingredients.prepNote: such as sea bass or bream, 180g each

steps.text: Make chermoula by blending coriander, parsley, garlic, cumin, paprika, cayenne, lemon juice, and olive oil in a food processor until smooth. Season with salt.
Place fish fillets in a baking dish. Coat generously with chermoula, reserving 3 tablespoons. Marinate for 10 minutes.
Preheat oven to 200°C. Bake fish for 15-18 minutes until cooked through and flaking easily.
Serve fish over couscous, drizzled with reserved chermoula and lemon wedges on the side.

title: Tunisian Brik with Egg and Tuna
shortDescription: Crispy phyllo parcels with egg, tuna, capers, and harissa
note: Eat immediately while the egg is still runny
introCopy: Brik is Tunisia's favorite street food - ultra-crispy pastry filled with a whole egg that stays runny inside. Breaking into it is the best part.

steps.text: Mix tuna with capers, spring onions, parsley, and harissa. Season with salt and pepper.
Take 2 sheets of phyllo and place them slightly offset to create a larger surface. Place a quarter of the tuna mixture on one side, leaving a border.
Make a small well in the tuna mixture. Carefully crack an egg into the well, keeping the yolk intact.
Fold the phyllo over to form a half-moon, pressing edges to seal tightly. Repeat with remaining phyllo and filling to make 4 briks.
Heat oil in a large frying pan over medium-high heat (about 2cm deep). Fry each brik for 2-3 minutes per side until golden and crisp. The egg white should set but yolk remain runny.
Drain on paper towels and serve immediately with lemon wedges.

title: Egyptian Koshari
shortDescription: Layered rice, lentils, pasta, and chickpeas with spiced tomato sauce
note: Egypt's beloved street food - hearty and completely vegan
introCopy: Koshari is Cairo's ultimate comfort food: a glorious mix of rice, lentils, pasta, and chickpeas topped with spicy tomato sauce and crispy fried onions.

steps.text: Cook lentils in boiling water for 20 minutes until tender. Drain. Cook rice according to package instructions. Cook pasta until al dente. Heat chickpeas.
For the sauce: heat olive oil in a pan. Add garlic and cook for 1 minute. Add tomatoes, vinegar, cumin, and cayenne. Simmer for 15 minutes until thickened. Season with salt.

For crispy onions: heat vegetable oil in a frying pan. Fry onions in batches, stirring frequently, until deep golden brown and crispy, about 12 minutes per batch. Drain on paper towels and sprinkle with salt.
To assemble: layer rice in serving bowls. Top with lentils, then pasta, then chickpeas.
Pour hot tomato sauce over each bowl and top generously with crispy onions. Serve immediately.

title: Egyptian Ful Medames
shortDescription: Slow-cooked fava beans with garlic, lemon, and olive oil
note: Egypt's national breakfast dish
introCopy: Ful medames has sustained Egyptians for thousands of years. These creamy fava beans flavored with garlic, cumin, and lemon are simple perfection.

steps.text: Heat fava beans in a pot with about 100ml of their reserved liquid. Simmer gently for 10 minutes.
Mash about half the beans roughly with a potato masher, leaving the rest whole. Stir in garlic and cumin. Cook for 2 minutes.
Remove from heat. Stir in lemon juice and half the olive oil. Season generously with salt and pepper.
Divide ful among bowls. Drizzle with remaining olive oil. Top with tomatoes, red onion, and parsley.
Serve with hard-boiled eggs if using and warm pita bread for scooping.

title: Moroccan Msemen Flatbread
shortDescription: Flaky layered flatbread cooked on a griddle
note: Serve warm with honey and butter for breakfast
introCopy: Msemen are Morocco's beloved square flatbreads with layers of flaky goodness. They're folded and cooked on a griddle until golden and crisp outside, tender inside.

steps.text: Mix flour, semolina, salt, and sugar in a large bowl. Gradually add warm water, kneading to form a soft, slightly sticky dough. Knead for 10 minutes until smooth and elastic.
Divide dough into 8 equal balls. Coat each with oil and let rest covered for 20 minutes.
Mix melted butter with vegetable oil. On an oiled surface, flatten each ball and stretch it into a very thin rectangle (almost translucent), using your fingers.
Brush the stretched dough generously with the butter-oil mixture. Fold in thirds lengthwise, then fold in thirds again to create a square. Let rest for 10 minutes.
Heat a griddle or large frying pan over medium heat. Gently flatten each square slightly and cook for 3-4 minutes per side until golden brown with crispy edges.
Serve warm with honey and butter.

title: Zaalouk - Moroccan Eggplant Dip
shortDescription: Smoky roasted eggplant and tomato salad with cumin and paprika
note: Serve as part of a mezze spread with bread
introCopy: Zaalouk is Morocco's addictive eggplant salad, cooked down with tomatoes, garlic, and warm spices until jammy and rich. Perfect for dipping bread.

steps.text: Prick eggplants all over with a fork. Roast over an open flame or under a hot grill, turning regularly, until skin is charred and flesh is very soft, about 20 minutes. Let cool.
Peel away charred skin and roughly chop the flesh. Discard excess liquid.
Heat olive oil in a large pan over medium heat. Add garlic and cook for 1 minute. Add cumin, paprika, coriander, and cayenne. Cook for 1 minute.
Add eggplant and tomatoes. Cook, stirring frequently and breaking up the eggplant, for 15 minutes until mixture is thick and jammy.
Remove from heat. Stir in lemon juice and fresh coriander. Season generously with salt and pepper.
Serve warm or at room temperature with crusty bread. Zaalouk keeps well in the fridge for up to 5 days.

title: Taktouka - Moroccan Pepper and Tomato Salad
shortDescription: Roasted peppers and tomatoes cooked into a smoky dip
note: Delicious warm or cold as part of a mezze
introCopy: Taktouka is a Moroccan cooked salad where charred peppers and tomatoes are simmered with garlic and spices into a silky, smoky dip.

steps.text: Char peppers over an open flame or under a hot grill until blackened all over, about 15 minutes. Place in a covered bowl to steam for 10 minutes, then peel, deseed, and dice.
Score tomatoes, blanch in boiling water for 1 minute, then peel and dice.
Heat olive oil in a large pan. Add garlic and cook for 1 minute. Add cumin, paprika, and cayenne if using. Cook for 30 seconds.
Add peppers and tomatoes. Cook over medium heat, stirring occasionally, for 20 minutes until mixture has thickened and flavors have melded.
Stir in fresh parsley. Season with salt and pepper. Serve warm or at room temperature with bread.

title: Moroccan Beef Kefta Tagine
shortDescription: Spiced meatballs in rich tomato sauce with eggs
note: The eggs poached on top make this extra special
introCopy: Kefta tagine features seasoned beef meatballs cooked in a fragrant tomato sauce, finished with eggs poached right in the sauce. It's pure comfort.

steps.text: Mix beef mince with grated onion, parsley, coriander, cumin, paprika, cinnamon, and salt. Form into walnut-sized meatballs (about 20).
Heat olive oil in a tagine or large deep pan. Add chopped onion and cook until softened, 8 minutes. Add garlic and cook for 1 minute.
Add tomatoes, paprika, and cumin. Simmer for 10 minutes until sauce has thickened. Season with salt and pepper.
Nestle meatballs into the sauce. Cover and simmer gently for 15 minutes until meatballs are cooked through.
Make 4 wells in the sauce between meatballs. Crack an egg into each well. Cover and cook for 5 minutes until egg whites are set but yolks still runny.
Serve immediately with couscous.

title: Algerian Chorba
shortDescription: Hearty lamb and vegetable soup with vermicelli and chickpeas
note: A Ramadan favorite throughout Algeria
introCopy: Chorba is Algeria's beloved soup, rich with lamb, vegetables, and aromatic spices. It's traditionally the first thing eaten to break the fast during Ramadan.

steps.text: Heat olive oil in a large pot. Brown lamb on all sides, about 8 minutes. Remove and set aside.
Add onions and celery to the pot. Cook until softened, about 8 minutes. Add cumin, coriander, paprika, and cinnamon. Cook for 1 minute.
Return lamb to pot. Add carrots, turnip, tomatoes, tomato paste, chickpeas, and stock. Bring to a boil.
Reduce heat and simmer covered for 60 minutes until lamb is very tender and vegetables are soft.
Add vermicelli and cook for 5 minutes until tender. Stir in fresh coriander. Season with salt and pepper.
Serve hot with lemon wedges for squeezing.

title: Moroccan Couscous with Tfaya
shortDescription: Sweet caramelized onions with raisins and cinnamon over couscous
note: Tfaya is the ultimate sweet-savory Moroccan topping
introCopy: Tfaya is Morocco's magical caramelized onion topping, slow-cooked with raisins, honey, and warm spices. It's traditionally served over chicken and couscous for celebrations.

steps.text: Heat olive oil in a large pot. Season chicken with ginger, saffron, salt, and pepper. Brown chicken pieces, about 8 minutes. Add stock and simmer covered for 35 minutes until tender.
Meanwhile, make tfaya: heat olive oil in a large pan. Add onions and cook over medium-low heat, stirring regularly, for 30 minutes until very soft and golden.
Add cinnamon, ginger, raisins, and honey to the onions. Continue cooking for 15 minutes until onions are caramelized and sticky. Stir in toasted almonds.
Mound couscous on a large serving platter. Arrange chicken pieces on top. Spoon tfaya over the chicken.
Drizzle with some of the chicken cooking liquid and serve immediately.

title: Moroccan Bissara - Fava Bean Soup
shortDescription: Creamy dried fava bean soup with cumin and olive oil
note: A warming winter breakfast in Morocco
introCopy: Bissara is Morocco's silky fava bean soup, finished with a generous drizzle of olive oil and dusting of cumin. It's simple, nourishing, and utterly comforting.

steps.text: Drain soaked fava beans. Place in a large pot with garlic and water. Bring to a boil.
Reduce heat and simmer for 50-60 minutes until beans are completely tender and falling apart.
Add cumin and paprika. Blend the soup until completely smooth using an immersion blender or regular blender. The consistency should be like thick cream.
Season generously with salt. If too thick, add a little water.
Ladle into bowls. Drizzle generously with olive oil and sprinkle with cumin and paprika. Serve hot with crusty bread.

title: Basbousa - Semolina Cake
shortDescription: Sweet semolina cake soaked in orange blossom syrup
note: Popular across North Africa and the Middle East
introCopy: Basbousa is a beloved North African dessert - a tender semolina cake soaked in fragrant syrup. Each piece is studded with an almond and utterly irresistible.

steps.text: Preheat oven to 180°C. Grease and line a 23x33cm baking tin.
Mix semolina, sugar, coconut, and baking powder in a large bowl. Add melted butter, yogurt, eggs, and vanilla. Mix until well combined.
Pour into prepared tin and smooth the top. Cut into diamond or square shapes (don't cut all the way through). Press an almond into the center of each piece.
Bake for 35-40 minutes until golden brown and a skewer comes out clean.
While cake bakes, make syrup: combine sugar, water, and lemon juice in a pan. Bring to a boil, then simmer for 10 minutes. Remove from heat and stir in orange blossom water.
As soon as the cake comes out of the oven, pour the hot syrup evenly over it. Let it soak in completely as the cake cools.
Once cool, cut along the scored lines and serve. Basbousa keeps well for 5 days.

title: Chebakia - Moroccan Sesame Honey Cookies
shortDescription: Fried flower-shaped cookies coated in honey and sesame
note: A Ramadan specialty requiring patience and skill
introCopy: Chebakia are Morocco's most intricate cookies - delicate dough shaped into flowers, fried until crisp, then soaked in warm honey and coated with sesame seeds.

steps.text: Mix flour, ground sesame, cinnamon, and anise in a large bowl. Make a well in the center.
Add eggs, saffron water, orange blossom water, oil, and vinegar to the well. Gradually incorporate flour until a smooth, elastic dough forms. Knead for 10 minutes. Rest for 30 minutes.
Roll dough very thin (2mm). Cut into rectangles about 10x6cm. Make 4 lengthwise slits in each rectangle, leaving the ends intact. Fold into a flower shape by weaving strips through each other.
Heat oil for frying to 170°C. Fry chebakia in batches until golden brown, about 3 minutes per batch. Drain on paper towels.
Warm honey in a wide pan. Dip each fried chebakia in honey for 10 seconds, coating well. Remove and immediately coat with sesame seeds.
Let chebakia dry on a rack. Store in an airtight container for up to 2 weeks.

title: Libyan Bazeen
shortDescription: Traditional barley dough served with rich lamb and tomato stew
note: Eaten communally, breaking pieces from the central dome
introCopy: Bazeen is Libya's national dish - a smooth barley dough dome surrounded by a rich lamb and vegetable stew. It's traditionally eaten with your hands.

steps.text: Heat olive oil in a large pot. Brown lamb cubes on all sides, about 10 minutes. Remove and set aside.
Add onions to the pot and cook until softened, 8 minutes. Add garlic, cumin, and paprika. Cook for 1 minute.
Return lamb to pot. Add tomatoes, tomato paste, potatoes, carrots, and stock. Bring to a boil, then simmer covered for 60 minutes until lamb is very tender.
Meanwhile, make bazeen: bring salted water to a boil in a large pot. Gradually add barley flour while stirring constantly with a wooden spoon to prevent lumps.
Reduce heat to low. Continue stirring vigorously for 15-20 minutes until mixture is very thick, smooth, and pulls away from the sides of the pot. This requires significant arm strength.
Form the hot bazeen into a smooth dome shape on a large serving platter using wet hands or a wet spoon.
Arrange lamb and vegetables around the bazeen dome. Pour stew sauce over everything. Serve immediately, breaking off pieces of bazeen to dip in the stew.

title: Moroccan Rfissa
shortDescription: Shredded msemen with chicken, lentils, and fenugreek sauce
note: Traditionally served to new mothers for strength
introCopy: Rfissa is a deeply nourishing Moroccan dish of tender chicken and lentils over shredded flatbread, all infused with the distinctive flavor of fenugreek and ras el hanout.

steps.text: Toast fenugreek seeds in a dry pan until fragrant, about 2 minutes. Grind to a powder.
Place chicken in a large pot with onions, ground fenugreek, ras el hanout, ginger, saffron, butter, and stock. Bring to a boil.
Reduce heat and simmer covered for 45 minutes until chicken is tender. Remove chicken and set aside.
Add lentils to the pot. Simmer for 25 minutes until lentils are tender and sauce has reduced.
Shred the chicken, discarding bones. Return meat to the pot with fresh coriander. Season with salt and pepper.
Tear msemen into bite-sized pieces. Arrange on a large platter. Ladle the chicken, lentils, and plenty of sauce over the bread. Let it soak for 5 minutes before serving.

title: Tunisian Slata Mechouia
shortDescription: Grilled vegetable salad with peppers, tomatoes, and tuna
note: A classic Tunisian mezze - smoky, spicy, and addictive
introCopy: Slata mechouia means grilled salad in Tunisian Arabic. Charred peppers and tomatoes are finely chopped and mixed with tuna, capers, and olive oil for an intensely flavorful dip.

steps.text: Grill or broil peppers, tomatoes, chillies, and garlic until charred all over, about 20 minutes. Place peppers and chillies in a covered bowl to steam for 10 minutes.
Peel and deseed peppers and chillies. Peel tomatoes and squeeze out excess seeds. Peel garlic.
Finely chop all the grilled vegetables and garlic by hand or pulse briefly in a food processor - you want a coarse texture, not a puree.
Transfer to a bowl. Add tuna, capers, caraway seeds, ground coriander, olive oil, and lemon juice. Mix well. Season generously with salt.
Let sit for at least 30 minutes for flavors to meld. Serve at room temperature, garnished with hard-boiled egg quarters if using. Accompany with crusty bread.

title: Moroccan Maakouda - Potato Fritters
shortDescription: Crispy fried potato patties with cumin and parsley
note: Perfect as a snack or served in sandwiches
introCopy: Maakouda are Morocco's beloved potato fritters - crispy on the outside, fluffy inside, and flavored with cumin, parsley, and garlic. Often served in sandwiches or as mezze.

steps.text: Boil potatoes in salted water for 15-20 minutes until very tender. Drain well and mash until smooth. Let cool slightly.
Add garlic, parsley, coriander, cumin, and paprika to the mashed potatoes. Mix well. Season generously with salt and pepper.
Stir in beaten eggs, then add flour gradually until mixture is firm enough to shape but still moist.
Shape mixture into small patties about 6cm wide and 1.5cm thick. You should get about 16 patties.
Heat oil in a large frying pan over medium-high heat (about 2cm deep). Fry patties in batches for 3-4 minutes per side until golden brown and crispy. Drain on paper towels.
Serve hot with harissa for dipping and lemon wedges. Maakouda are also excellent in sandwiches with salad and harissa.

title: Egyptian Mahshi - Stuffed Vegetables
shortDescription: Tomatoes, peppers, and courgettes stuffed with herbed rice
note: A labor of love that's worth every minute
introCopy: Mahshi means stuffed in Arabic. This Egyptian version features vegetables filled with aromatic rice, herbs, and sometimes meat, then simmered in tomato broth until tender.

steps.text: Prepare vegetables: slice tops off tomatoes and peppers, scoop out insides (save tomato flesh for sauce). Trim courgette ends and hollow out centers with an apple corer, leaving 0.5cm walls.
Make filling: mix rice, mince if using, onion, parsley, dill, tomato paste, cumin, coriander, and olive oil. Season generously with salt and pepper.
Stuff vegetables about 3/4 full with filling (rice will expand). Replace tomato and pepper tops.
Arrange stuffed vegetables snugly in a large pot. Mix blended tomatoes, stock, tomato paste, and garlic. Pour over vegetables - liquid should come halfway up.
Place an inverted plate on top of vegetables to keep them submerged. Bring to a boil, then reduce heat to low. Cover and simmer for 60 minutes until vegetables are tender and rice is cooked.
Carefully transfer mahshi to serving plates. Spoon sauce over the top. Serve hot with crusty bread or alongside a salad.
